title: Leading great teaching
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart starts from the claim that every school already has a pedagogical framework, whether or not anyone wrote it down, because it lives in repeated routines, praised habits and corridor conversation. His argument is that the value of a good framework - he uses Evidence Based Education's model for great teaching - lies in reducing misinterpretation, and that the way to get that value is to translate the framework into how teachers here already talk rather than simply adopt it. Schein's three levels of culture supply the reason: school improvement usually works on what teachers do and say while leaving beliefs untouched, so an imported framework bypasses sense-making and does not survive. He then separates teaching from learning, warning that quality judgements drift into checking whether advocated strategies were used rather than whether children understood, and proposes self-efficacy as the north star the domains serve. The essay's central distinction is coherence versus consistency: consistency is defensible where varied routines would push cognitive load onto decoding each teacher's expectations, while coherence means agreement on why a strategy is used rather than a sanctioned script. Because learning is invisible in a lesson, he ends by arguing leaders need indicators for whether great teaching on paper is producing learning, while conceding a paradox in how heavily he weights relationships and routines against hard thinking.
points: Hart's translation-over-adoption rule is the practical core: a framework worded in someone else's language cannot be enacted, because implementation is a sense-making problem before it is a compliance one.
He names the specific failure of low-implementation schools - professional learning as a carousel of strategies that lose momentum whenever the next idea arrives.
The teaching-versus-learning confusion is diagnosed through the tick-box reflex: retrieval starter, tick; I do, we do, you do, tick - none of which evidences understanding.
Consistency is justified on cognitive-load grounds (Peps McCrea's norm alignment) rather than on managerial preference, which tells leaders which practices actually warrant uniformity.
Because a strategy only worked in the context where it was established, coherence asks for alignment on goals and a mindset of adaptation rather than identical minute-by-minute practice.
quotes: It lives in existing practice; the routines teachers repeat because they matter, the habits leaders praise, the mental models that get passed around in corridor conversations. Sometimes that framework is consciously built and shared, and sometimes it is accidentally assembled through inference.

Great pedagogical frameworks implemented well do something deceptively simple: they reduce the likelihood of misinterpretation. And an example of a great pedagogical framework is the model for great teaching from Evidence Based Education.

There’s an optimism that comes with finding a model that makes sense on paper. The excitement often carries us straight past the considerations of: What would this sound like here, in this school, spoken by our teachers, about our children?

It sounds absurd, but in schools we blur these two all the time. When we make judgements on the quality of teaching, it is easy to focus on whether teachers employed the strategies we advocate rather than the extent to which those strategies made a difference to children’s understanding.
Coherence works differently. It requires alignment on goals and and the mindset of adaptation. We agree why we use retrieval, not exactly how it should look minute-by-minute.
But learning is invisible. We can’t see it in a lesson. Children might be performing well but this is not the same as learning.
